theory_query: How does reconstructing gridded daily dew-point temperature from daily minimum temperature, using per-climate-zone and per-day-of-year weighted local linear regression on climate anomalies with autoregressive dew-point lags, affect (i) reconstruction accuracy and (ii) the physical plausibility of the resulting dew-point field, across contrasting climate zones of Peru (hyper-arid coast, high Andes, humid Amazon lowlands)? Two mechanisms are of interest. (a) SKILL: what mechanism explains why such localized per-zone, per-day-of-year tuning substantially outperforms daily climatology and the FAO-56 Tdew approximately equals Tmin assumption, and why model selection favours very wide (45-day) day-of-year smoothing windows rather than narrow seasonal windows? What does a preference for broad day-of-year pooling imply physically about the coupling between nocturnal minimum temperature and dew point? (b) FAILURE: what mechanism produces unphysically high reconstructed dew points (above 35 degrees C) that are spatially confined to the north-eastern Amazon lowlands and temporally confined to the late dry season (August to October)?
mission_statement: Scope: statistical reconstruction and temporal gap-filling of gridded humidity fields from temperature in tropical South America. Prioritise evidence on: (1) the physical coupling between nocturnal minimum temperature and dew point and the conditions under which it breaks down (aridity, elevation, humid lowlands, soil moisture and boundary-layer controls); (2) physical upper bounds on dew point and dew-point behaviour near saturation in the humid tropics; (3) late-dry-season Amazon humidity dynamics including drought, biomass burning, and land-atmosphere coupling; (4) error growth and drift in autoregressive multi-step prediction of climate variables; (5) validation practice for temporally extended gridded climate products, including choice of baselines such as climatology. Output should be usable as discussion-section material contrasting our results with prior work.
